skript.thema: Claude Projects: workspaces, instructions and the new beta

teile.name: Hook
teile.text: Stop re-explaining your work, because Claude can remember it for you. Projects are self-contained workspaces, each with its own chat history and knowledge base.
teile.szene: Black-haired presenter in black leather jacket and glowing cyan glasses at a desk, rubbing his forehead while looking at a laptop, painted open-world-game poster style, medium shot, warm evening lamp light.

teile.name: Knowledge base
teile.text: Upload documents, text, code or other files. Claude uses them as background context for your individual chats inside that project.
teile.szene: Official Claude Help Center page on projects, showing the description of uploading documents, text, code or other files to a project's knowledge base.

teile.name: Instructions
teile.text: Then add project instructions. Ask for a formal tone, or answers from the perspective of a specific role or industry.
teile.szene: Cyan-glasses presenter in black leather jacket typing thoughtfully on a laptop, seen over his shoulder at a cluttered desk, warm lamp light, painted urban game-poster style, medium shot.

teile.name: Plans and limits
teile.text: Free accounts can create up to five projects. Paid plans add RAG, which expands project capacity when knowledge nears context limits.
teile.szene: Help Center excerpt about free users having a maximum of five projects and RAG being available only on paid plans for larger project knowledge.

teile.name: New beta
teile.text: So what's changing? A beta version makes a project one conversation, and Claude splits work into parallel cloud threads.
teile.szene: Presenter in black leather jacket and cyan glasses leaning back in his chair with a surprised, intrigued look, city skyline glowing through the window behind him, painted open-world-game poster style, wide shot, cool blue light.

teile.name: The catch
teile.text: The catch: it's beta, rolling out in stages. Still, files and instructions stay in the project, so you stop re-explaining.
teile.szene: Presenter in black leather jacket and cyan glasses relaxing back at his desk with a calm, satisfied smile, laptop open beside him, painted open-world-game poster style, medium shot, warm lamp light.

teile.name: Ending
teile.text: Be sure to like, share and save this video.
teile.szene: Cyan-glasses presenter in black leather jacket smiling at a tidy desk with a closed laptop beside him, painted game-poster style, medium shot, warm light.

regeln: Within each spoken phase use multiple distinct relevant shots, roughly 3-5 seconds each for Shorts; long videos can allow purposeful longer demonstrations. Preserve continuous narration and accurate subtitle timing.
A zoom, crop, subtitle change or decorative background does not count as a new motif. Never fill missing images with candles, unrelated stock or background-only frames.
Show the main image prominently; avoid tiny repeated photos in a mostly empty vertical frame. Preserve genuine evidence and important image details.
For AI Tools Explained identify the exact tool briefly, then show genuine interface views and different source-supported examples. Never present stock or an illustration as a real tool result.
Use original urban painted open-world-game poster styling for fictional scenes and presenters; no copied game characters. Match narrated action and era.

Clear speech and readable captions alone do not make a professional video. Inspect useful motif changes and narration-image alignment over the entire video. Missing main imagery is a substantial defect.
Include mandatory spoken like, share and save calls at the correct format-specific positions. Do not replace this requirement with a different CTA.

AI Tools Explained is for viewers with a practical task. Do not read parameter counts, architecture names, pipeline tags, context lengths or benchmark claims as a substitute for useful explanation. Explain the human task, the source-supported action and a concrete limit. A generic trending-tools question failed story review twice; prefer a specific visual workflow.

The user confirmed original presenter references on 2026-10-05: Business Origin Stories uses the blue-eyed man with a fedora, grey suit, dark tie and gold pocket watch; AI Tools Explained uses the black-haired man with black leather jacket and glowing cyan glasses. Preserve identity and typical clothing, vary action and setting.

Introduce the correct presenter at the opening and bring that same presenter back during the video in useful actions. Do not confine the figure to the ending. Do not replace original channel figures with different fictional people; anonymous period workers remain clearly illustrative supporting people, never a real-founder likeness.

Prefer vivid original painted open-world-game scenes to long holds on lifeless documentary photos. Preserve factual accuracy and show authentic tool examples briefly as evidence. Camera moves alone are not new motifs or full character animation.

The user confirmed on 2026-10-05 that both new delivered videos are much better than before. Preserve the original painted world, recurring channel identity, matching main imagery, music and useful scene changes. The long-term quality target remains 10/10; the user did not give these videos a numeric score. Do not replace their actual AI scores or the existing 7/10 delivery threshold with the aspirational target.

Match each spoken claim with concrete, source-supported visual evidence such as tool UIs, configuration screens, diagrams, or screenshots; never rely on generic icons, stock images, illustrative placeholders, or plain text graphics.
Preserve continuous narration with accurately timed subtitles and keep the main imagery prominent and directly relevant to the spoken words.
Include the mandatory spoken CTA (like, share, save) at the format-specific position without alteration.
Link technical features to the initial human task or character introduced, keeping a narrative anchor that ties explanations back to practical use.
Show the exact AI tool being discussed briefly, then display authentic interface views, software diagrams, and real-world examples that support the narration.
Use comparative tables or diagrams to visualize tool choices, file interactions, or sandbox environments instead of generic code blocks or plain titles.
Respect format-specific pacing: do not apply Shorts-style speed to long-form videos or long-form pacing to Shorts.
When a review suggests a fix, implement the concrete observable correction but treat the feedback as provisional data; avoid overgeneralizing a single defect into a blanket rule.
Introduce the correct presenter at the opening and bring the same presenter back for useful actions later in the video; do not limit the presenter to only the ending.
Avoid weakening language that reduces narrative immediacy; state scenarios directly when the facts are accurate.

What are projects? | Claude Help Center
Note: A new version of projects is now available in beta, rolling out in stages starting with Claude Code. We've started moving existing projects for some Pro and Max users to the new version. See The new version of projects (beta) below.
Projects allow you to create self-contained workspaces with their own chat histories and knowledge bases. Within each project, you can upload documents, provide context, and have focused chats with Claude.
Projects are available to all users, including those with free Claude accounts. Free users can create a maximum of five projects.
The new version of projects (beta)
We're rolling out a new version of projects in stages, starting with Claude Code. In the new version, a project is one conversation: you say what you need as it comes to you, and Claude breaks the work into parallel threads that run in the cloud. Claude tells you what's done and what's waiting on you, and if you close your laptop, the threads keep going. Every thread starts with the project's files, repositories, instructions, and memory, and the project's Library collects the files you add and the files Claude produces.
The new version is now available in beta to select Pro and Max subscribers who use Claude Code, and to some Pro and Max users whose existing projects we’ve moved to the new version. If you have it, you'll see "Projects" in the sidebar at claude.ai/code and in the Code tab of the Claude desktop app. More Claude Code users on Pro and Max plans will get access as the rollout expands, and chat, Cowork, Team, and Enterprise will follow. If you're on Pro or Max and don't have access yet, you can join the waitlist .
We’ve started moving existing projects for some Pro and Max users to the new version. Nothing is lost or deleted in the move. Everything in your project comes with it: your instructions, files, full chat history, and scheduled tasks. You’ll pick up right where you left off. If you've used an existing project within the last 30 days, we’ll email you before we move your projects. Other existing projects in chat and Cowork stay on the current version for now, and we’ll move them as the rollout expands.
Projects draw from your plan's usage like any other use of Claude, and running several threads at once uses it faster.
For more on the new version, see Projects in the Claude Code docs. The rest of this article describes the current version of projects.
A key benefit of projects is the ability to provide context for your chats with Claude. You can upload relevant documents, text, code, or other files to a project's knowledge base, which Claude will use to better understand the context and background for your individual chats within that project.
In addition, you can define project instructions for each project to further tailor Claude's responses. For example, instructing Claude to use a more formal tone or answer questions from the perspective of a specific role or industry.
Enhanced project knowledge with RAG is only available to users with paid Claude plans (Pro, Max, Team, or Enterprise).
When using a paid plan, your projects automatically scale to handle large amounts of content through Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG). When your project knowledge approaches context limits, Claude seamlessly enables RAG mode to expand capacity by up to 10x while maintaining response quality.
For more information on leveraging expanded project knowledge capacity, see Retrieval augmented generation (RAG) for projects .
Collaboration and sharing (Team and Enterprise plans only)
For users on Team and Enterprise plans, projects can be shared with other members of your organization, enabling powerful collaboration and knowledge sharing capabilities. The sharing system includes:
Can view: Members can see project contents, knowledge, and instructions, and chat within the project, but cannot edit it.
Can edit: Members can modify project instructions and knowledge, add/remove members, update member settings, and actively contribute to the project.
Share to specific members instead of making a project fully private or public to the entire organization.
Make a previously-created private project visible to the whole organization.
Individual sharing: Share projects with specific team members by email.
Bulk sharing: Add multiple users at once using email lists.
Organization-wide sharing: Make projects available to everyone in your organization either when creating the project or afterward.
Note: If an Owner or Primary Owner disables public projects, organization-wide sharing will be disabled both when creating the project and afterward.
Admin controls: Owners can turn off project sharing for your organization, or on Enterprise plans for specific roles. Turning off Share projects also turns off Public projects . When sharing is off, users can't share projects with new users or groups, and existing shares stay in place.
Shared with me tab: Easily find projects that others have shared with you.
Email notifications: Get notified when someone shares a project with you.
Access management: Project creators can modify permissions or remove access as needed.
Multiple members can contribute documents, create chats, and work together within the same project environment, making projects ideal for team collaboration.
For more information on getting started with projects, see How can I create and manage projects?
For more information on private projects and visibility settings on Team and Enterprise plans, see Project visibility and sharing .

belege.name: Google Ads
belege.text:
Google Ads, formerly known as Google AdWords, is an online advertising platform developed by Google, where advertisers bid to display brief digital advertisements, service offerings, product listings, and videos to web users. It can place ads in the results of search engines like Google Search (the Google Search Network), mobile apps, videos, and on non-search websites. Services are offered under a pay-per-click (PPC) pricing model, and a cost-per-view (CPV) pricing model.


History: 
Google launched AdWords in year 2000. Initially, Google itself would set up and manage advertisers' campaigns. Google then introduced a self-service AdWords portal for small businesses that wanted to manage their own campaigns.
In 2005, Google started a campaign management service known as "Jumpstart".
In January 2006 Google purchased the radio advertising company dMarc Broadcasting.
In 2007, Google acquired DoubleClick for $3.1 billion. The acquisition was strategically important for Google, providing access to DoubleClick's advanced ad-serving technology and established industry relationships. This deal, while "transforming Google into a powerhouse", later attracted antitrust scrutiny, raising questions about its impact on market competition and digital advertising dominance.
In 2008, Google launched the Google Online Marketing Challenge, an in-class academic exercise for tertiary students.
Google retired the DoubleClick and AdWords brands in 2018 to simplify entry points for advertisers and ad sellers. The core product was renamed Google Ads, providing access to inventory on Google Search, its YouTube video service, the Google Play app store, and AdSense website publisher partners.

[Claude Tag] Fixed Claude Tag treating ! commands such as !restart and !help as ordinary messages when sent in bold, italic or strikethrough
[Claude Tag] Fixed Claude Tag admin channel and workspace pages being replaced by a load error when a background refresh of the bundle list fails

[Code Review] Fixed the Code Review admin section hiding its repositories and switches after a failed refresh of the repository list
[VSCode] Added a log warning that says what to do when dictation or the extension’s own requests fail certificate verification, such as behind a TLS-inspecting proxy
Updated the bundled dataviz skill to accept APCA as a text-contrast measure (keeping WCAG 2 ratios where AA conformance is required), add an apca(text, background) function to its palette validator scripts, and say whether a label inside a colored chart fill should be white or near-black
Updated the /claude-api skill: service account keys and Workload Identity Federation tokens can now manage OpenTelemetry destinations

Changed the dangerous rm and rmdir prompt in bypass permissions mode in the Desktop app and VS Code to deny the command at once with a rewrite hint, so unattended sessions keep going

belege.name: Google Antigravity
belege.text:
Google Antigravity is a software development platform from Google in which artificial intelligence (AI) agents write, run and test code with varying degrees of autonomy. It was released on November 18, 2025, alongside the Gemini 3 model, as an integrated development environment (IDE) that developers found to be derived from Visual Studio Code (VS Code). In May 2026, Google added Antigravity 2.0, a standalone desktop application for managing agents, together with a command-line interface (CLI) and a software development kit (SDK). The original editor continues as a separate product, the Antigravity IDE.
Antigravity uses Google's Gemini models and also offers models from Anthropic and OpenAI. It can be used free of charge within usage limits, which are higher for subscribers to Google's paid AI plans. Its launch prompted debate over whether it was a fork of VS Code or of Windsurf, an AI code editor whose technology Google had licensed earlier in 2025. In the months after launch, security researchers reported several vulnerabilities; Google responded with a stricter security mode, sandboxing for agent commands, and fixes for reported flaws.


History: 

Background: In July 2025, Google hired Varun Mohan, the chief executive of the AI coding startup Windsurf, along with co-founder Douglas Chen and several researchers, and paid $2.4 billion to license Windsurf's technology. The rest of Windsurf was acquired days later by Cognition AI. Mohan joined Google DeepMind as a director of software engineering and co-authored Google's announcement of Antigravity 2.0 in 2026.


Launch: Google announced Antigravity on November 18, 2025, the day it released Gemini 3, and made it available the same day as a free public preview for Windows, macOS and Linux. Google described it as an "agent-first" platform and offered "generous rate limits" on Gemini 3 Pro, which refreshed every five hours. Anthropic's Claude Sonnet 4.5 and OpenAI's open-weight GPT-OSS model were also available.
The announcement did not say what code Antigravity was built on. Developers who examined it concluded that it was derived from VS Code, and some found references to Cascade, Windsurf's proprietary agent system, suggesting that it might derive from Windsurf, itself a VS Code fork.


Early updates: In December 2025, Google raised the rate limits for Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers and moved free users to a weekly limit. After security researchers reported flaws in the software, Google added an optional "Secure Mode" on December 8, 2025, in which the agent's actions require human review; it was renamed "strict mode" in February 2026. Between January and March 2026, Google added the option to run the agent's terminal commands in a sandbox on macOS and Linux. Gemini 3 Flash became available in Antigravity in December 2025, and Gemini 3.1 Pro in February 2026.
In February 2026, Google cut off users who had connected the third-party agent OpenClaw to Antigravity's backend, citing "a massive increase in malicious usage of the Antigravity backend that has tremendously degraded the quality of service". It later added a process for suspended accounts to request reinstatement.


Antigravity 2.0: At Google I/O on May 19, 2026, Google released Antigravity 2.0, a standalone desktop application in which users can run several agents in parallel, define custom subagent workflows, and schedule tasks to run in the background. Google's documentation describes it as the successor to the original release's Agent Manager that, unlike the Agent Manager, "functions independently of an IDE". Google also released the Antigravity CLI, which replaced its earlier Gemini CLI for consumers, and the Antigravity SDK.
The original application, which Google now calls "Antigravity 1.0", was relaunched at the same time as a separate product, the Antigravity IDE, with its version numbering restarted at 2.0.1 and a tool for importing settings, extensions and keybindings from Antigravity 1.0. As of October 2026, the IDE is not supported for enterprise customers, and its most recent release was in August 2026, while the desktop application and the CLI continued to receive frequent updates.
